1.4a — Movement I: Input, Direction, Vector

Movement is the first real algorithm you build, and it hides the whole AP model inside it: input → processing → output. Today you write the three lines that every game in this course is built on.

Predict First ~10 min

Before you type anything, read the shipped PlayerController.cs (Assets/Scripts) and find these lines in Update(): 

xDirection = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal"); // A/D or Left/Right Arrows
yDirection = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");   // W/S or Up/Down Arrows

xVector = new Vector2(xDirection * xSpeed * Time.deltaTime, 0);

transform.Translate(xVector);

Predict, in writing, before you run it: if xSpeed is 5, how far does the player move in one second of holding D? (Careful — the answer is not 5 pixels.) What does Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") return the instant you are not pressing anything?

Socratic

Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") returns 0, or a smooth ramp toward +1 (D) / -1 (A). Why is a smooth ramp better for movement than Input.GetKeyDown, which is just yes/no? What would the game feel like if it snapped between 0 and 1?

Build Lab ~25 min

Rebuild it yourself. Open PlayerController.cs and comment out (or delete) every line of Update(). Now bring movement back, one piece at a time, in this exact order — run the game after each step:

Step 1 — the variables. You need somewhere for input to live. These already exist at the top of the file — find them and explain to your neighbor what [SerializeField] is doing there (check the Inspector while the game is not running): 

[SerializeField] private float xSpeed = 5.0f;
[SerializeField] private float ySpeed = 5.0f;

private float xDirection;
private float yDirection;

Step 2 — read the input. Grab the player's intent: 

xDirection = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
yDirection = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

Run it. The player still does not move — but the game is already reading the player. Nothing happens with data until you use it: input is not behavior.

Step 3 — combine into a vector. Direction alone is free; speed alone is nothing. Their product, scaled by how long this frame lasted, is motion: 

xVector = new Vector2(xDirection * xSpeed * Time.deltaTime, 0);
yVector = new Vector2(0, yDirection * ySpeed * Time.deltaTime);

Step 4 — move.

transform.Translate(xVector);
transform.Translate(yVector);
Why Time.deltaTime? Update runs once per frame — 60 times a second on this laptop, 240 on a gaming monitor, maybe 25 on a friend's potato. Without deltaTime, the player would move xSpeed per frame: fast on good machines, slow on bad ones. Multiplying by the frame time makes it xSpeed per second, on every machine. Same input, same output, any hardware — that is the abstraction doing its job.

Bug Hunt: Break the movement on purpose

Make each bug, run it, describe what you see, then fix it:

  1. Change xSpeed to 0 in the Inspector. Which direction still works, and why doesn't changing the Inspector break the script?
  2. Delete just * Time.deltaTime from the xVector line. The player now moves about how many times faster at 60 fps?
  3. Swap the arguments: new Vector2(0, xDirection * xSpeed * Time.deltaTime). What did you break and what still works?
  4. Type Transform.Translate (capital T). What does the error mean?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Make it yours

  1. Give the player a different top speed horizontally than vertically (try 8 and 4). What games actually do this, and why would a designer want it?
  2. Set xSpeed to -5 in the Inspector and play. Describe what happens and why the animation still faces the right way.
  3. Press A and W at the same time. The player moves diagonally — is it faster than pure-right? (Measure: walk across the screen both ways and count seconds.) Games fix this with normalization — file that away for the turret unit.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Draw the pipeline: input → direction → × speed → × deltaTime → vector → Translate
  • Say what Input.GetAxis returns for A, D, and nothing (−1, +1, 0)
  • Explain Time.deltaTime to someone who has never coded
  • Explain why the Inspector can override xSpeed without touching the code
  • Break and fix a movement bug on purpose in under a minute
